title: Courts for AI Constitutions
gist: Frontier labs now govern model behavior with vague constitutional documents — Anthropic's runs 80 pages, OpenAI has published its own, Microsoft and Google DeepMind are rumored to be drafting theirs — but have no institution for interpreting them, so the authors propose an internal court inside each lab that takes user-flagged cases, publishes reasoned opinions, and compounds them into a synthetic common law fed back into training. The central commercial argument is that predictable, published model behavior becomes an enterprise sales asset once frontier models are capability-equivalent, and the design explicitly avoids Meta's Oversight Board failures of narrow non-precedential rulings, external independence, and part-time staff.

insights.claim: Anthropic governs Claude via a Constitution running roughly 80 pages of moral philosophy describing the virtues and character traits it wants the model to embody, OpenAI has published its own variant, and Microsoft and Google DeepMind are rumored to be drafting theirs.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Published model constitutions are becoming table stakes across all major labs — a new artifact class that enterprise buyers, regulators, and litigants will start reading and citing.
insights.quote: In it lie 80 pages of moral philosophy describing the virtues and character traits Anthropic would like its model to embody.
insights.locator: To make this judgement call, Claude refers back

insights.claim: Constitutional instructions are operationally vague — a rule saying a model can reserve independent action where evidence is overwhelming and stakes are extremely high leaves undefined what counts as overwhelming evidence, where extremely high stakes begin, and what independent action permits.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The gap between written AI principles and applied behavior is where deployment risk actually lives; audits of model docs alone tell a buyer nothing.
insights.quote: Claude can reserve independent action for cases where the evidence is overwhelming and the stakes are extremely high.
insights.locator: Yet these constitutional instructions remain relatively vague.

insights.claim: Knowing a model's written rules without knowing how they have been applied is as useless as knowing the text of the First Amendment without any subsequent precedents.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A sharp analogy for evaluating AI governance disclosures: demand applied case outcomes, not principles documents.
insights.quote: which is just as useful as knowing the words that make up the First Amendment without knowing any subsequent precedents
insights.locator: Users don’t know in advance how rules will be applied

insights.claim: There is currently no institutionalized mechanism inside labs to gradually refine model rules over time, so revisions happen only ad hoc after a major public backlash.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Model behavior policy is therefore event-driven and reputationally reactive — expect discontinuous, PR-triggered changes rather than smooth evolution, a source of deployment instability.
insights.quote: there is no institutionalized mechanism to gradually refine rules over time, absent a major public backlash causing ad hoc revisions
insights.locator: Worse yet, there is no institutionalized mechanism

insights.claim: Model rules are effectively frozen between releases, which is a clumsy way to govern systems that are themselves evolving quickly and being asked questions their authors could not have anticipated.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Behavior drift risk is concentrated at release boundaries — enterprises should version-pin models and test behavior at each upgrade rather than assume continuity.
insights.quote: Model rules in their current form are essentially frozen between releases.
insights.locator: Building a Living Constitution

insights.claim: Labs assemble a model-behavior production function comprising a constitution team writing high-level rules and baking them in through reinforcement learning cycles, a red team stress-testing whether values hold under fire, policy-specific teams handling concrete issues like erotica or political speech, and product teams ingesting user feedback.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete org-chart map of where AI behavior decisions are actually made — useful for anyone diligencing a lab's safety claims or targeting policy advocacy.
insights.quote: the whole assembly line needed to get models to act according to a preferred philosophy
insights.locator: Labs string together a variety of internal teams

insights.claim: The multi-team behavior process is structurally flawed because writing high-level principles generates ambiguities and conflicting principles with no set way of resolving them, and coordination across sporadically operating teams arguably produces unprincipled results.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Inconsistent model behavior is a process defect, not a model defect — meaning it is fixable by institutional design rather than by scaling compute.
insights.quote: Writing high-level principles leads to ambiguities, conflicting principles, and open-ended interpretation with no set way of resolving them.
insights.locator: Unfortunately, this process has some profound structural flaws.

insights.claim: AI models must make millions of judgment calls daily on questions such as whether a demand could create a biological hazard, whether a child's question pertains to self-harm, or whether a military request violates international norms, and these calls grow more consequential as models are integrated into hospital systems, national intelligence, and warfighting.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Sizes the interpretive surface area — high-stakes verticals are exactly where model behavior governance becomes a procurement gate.
insights.quote: deciding whether a particular demand could create a biological hazard, whether a child’s question pertains to self-harm, whether a military request violates international norms
insights.locator: These decisions matter.

insights.claim: Public debate is misallocated, focused almost entirely on what rules should bind models and paying almost no attention to how those principles are interpreted and applied.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The under-covered interpretive layer is where the next wave of AI governance regulation and litigation will land — an early positioning opportunity for policy and compliance vendors.
insights.quote: public debate has been stuck around what rules should bind models, paying almost no attention to how those principles are interpreted and applied
insights.locator: Yet even as these stakes rise

insights.claim: Case intake would run through a costless in-product button letting any user flag a model response in a few sentences without needing familiarity with the constitution, plus an option for the model itself to flag cases where it is uncertain how to apply its own rules.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A shippable product feature, not a policy abstraction — the first lab to add a constitutional flag button gets the case-law dataset first.
insights.quote: An easy, costless button, visible within the user interface, could let a user flag a model’s response.
insights.locator: In the common law, an injured party claims

insights.claim: The vast majority of flagged claims would be triaged automatically by AI screening for whether rules are unsettled by precedent, whether principles are in tension, and whether the case carries broad relevance, with an initial filter requiring a minimum number of users to flag the same issue.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: AI-assisted docket triage is what makes a private court economically viable at consumer scale — the bottleneck the Oversight Board never solved.
insights.locator: The vast majority of these claims could be triaged

insights.claim: The proposed court would be a human-staffed internal supreme court of perhaps five to seven full-time staff, large enough to allow disagreement, holding the ultimate certiorari-like decision on which cases to accept even though preselection is left to the model.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A five-to-seven-person full-time headcount is a trivial cost for a frontier lab, which makes this proposal unusually likely to be piloted.
insights.quote: perhaps five to seven staff members for whom this is their full-time job
insights.locator: Once a case is identified, it would go up to a

insights.claim: The AI court should be inquisitorial rather than adversarial, with judges investigating issues themselves like small claims courts and some administrative agency courts, avoiding a formal and burdensome litigious system.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Design choice that keeps throughput high and legal costs low — the difference between a functioning docket and Oversight-Board-style paralysis.
insights.locator: The one area where these courts might depart

insights.claim: The court must sit inside the lab rather than be independent, because understanding model behavior requires substantial technical know-how and because rulings are implemented by modifying model weights, which cannot be done from outside.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the prevailing independence-is-legitimacy assumption in tech governance; expect pushback from civil society but faster real-world adoption.
insights.quote: since rulings are used to modify the model weights—something that  cannot be done from the outside
insights.locator: As a default setup, the court would be composed

insights.claim: Court membership could eventually be drawn from outside third parties, government officials, public-interest representatives, or even be directly elected by users, inspired by the design of Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: User-elected governance of a model's values would be a genuinely novel corporate governance structure — worth tracking as a template if any lab adopts it.
insights.locator: That said, there’s room for more creative approaches

insights.claim: The court should invite public amicus briefs from moral philosophers, linguists, religious leaders, and impacted parties rather than restricting submissions to lawyers, formalizing the ad hoc consultations currently happening in the background.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Creates a public participation channel in AI values that could absorb regulatory pressure for democratic input without statutory mandates.
insights.locator: Importantly, this process could benefit from being open

insights.claim: Published court opinions would be used two ways: as training examples for the next model, and as a live dataset any model can consult in real time while wrestling with a dilemma.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The live-lookup path means behavior policy could update between model releases without retraining — a meaningful architectural implication for how labs ship values.
insights.quote: (a) to supply examples to train the next model and (b) as a live dataset that any model can refer to in real time as it wrestles with its next dilemma
insights.locator: These opinions would then accumulate into a corpus

insights.claim: Real-world users produce a much richer and stranger distribution of hard cases than any small group of internal researchers can anticipate, so any system relying solely on imagined hypotheticals will be out-imagined by reality.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A Hayekian argument that user-generated edge cases are a proprietary data asset — labs with the largest consumer user bases have a structural alignment-data advantage.
insights.quote: Any system that relies solely on imagined hypotheticals will be out-imagined by reality
insights.locator: Generating a Richer Training Corpus

insights.claim: Court rulings would form an unusually high-quality training corpus because they contain detailed explanations of how competing principles should be weighed plus step-by-step walkthroughs of exemplary moral reasoning.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reasoning-dense, hand-written adjudications are exactly the scarce data type labs pay most for — the court effectively becomes a data-generation function.
insights.quote: This new body of case law would create a gold mine with hundreds of high-quality examples for character training.
insights.locator: Importantly, the rulings themselves would be unusually high quality

insights.claim: An internal court acts as a pressure release valve that lets principles be frequently reexamined and progressively refined, making rule evolution structured rather than dependent on public relations backlash.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reduces the tail risk of abrupt, headline-driven model behavior changes that break enterprise workflows.
insights.quote: It creates a pressure release valve, through which existing principles are frequently reexamined
insights.locator: An internal court allows for rules to evolve

insights.claim: In a competitive market where frontier models have roughly similar capabilities, the ability to offer a predictable business environment where firms know in advance how a model will handle their cases is meaningful for enterprise customers dependent on stable behavior.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The commercial core of the argument: as capability converges, behavioral predictability becomes the enterprise differentiator and a defensible moat — watch which lab markets it first.
insights.quote: the ability to offer a more predictable business environment—one in which firms can know in advance how a model will handle their cases—is meaningful for enterprise customers dependent on stable behavior
insights.locator: Improving Transparency and Predictability

insights.claim: Gradual case-by-case rule evolution creates more short-term variation but is more stable long term than periodic top-down rewrites, the same way judicial review reduces the need for sudden constitutional overhauls.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reframes the tradeoff enterprises face: accept small continuous behavior drift to avoid large discontinuous policy shocks.
insights.locator: While allowing rules to evolve over time

insights.claim: Anthropic's Collective Constitutional AI experiment demonstrated the difficulty of producing actionable guidelines by asking the general public to agree on broad principles from scratch, whereas asking the public to react to narrow concrete cases is a far more tractable task.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A documented failure mode for democratic AI input; any regulator or lab designing public consultation should shift from principle-drafting to case-reaction formats.
insights.quote: Anthropic’s Collective Constitutional AI experiment was a clear example of the difficulty of producing actionable guidelines by asking the general public to agree on broad principles from scratch.
insights.locator: Giving the Public a Say

insights.claim: Published AI court opinions would perform a civic function analogous to what Alexis de Tocqueville saw in juries — a gratuitous public school that builds habits of civic autonomy — by turning model dilemmas into national arguments debated outside the lab.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Positions AI governance as civic infrastructure, which is the framing most likely to win political legitimacy for lab-run institutions.
insights.quote: gratuitous public school
insights.locator: Cultivating Public Deliberation

themes.theme: Why the Meta Oversight Board failed

insights.claim: Meta's Oversight Board largely failed because of scale: each content moderation decision was applied only to other posts containing identical content with parallel context, stripping rulings of precedential force so that correcting a few instances made little difference against billions of daily moderation decisions.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The precedent-scope design choice, not staffing or independence, is the first thing to check when evaluating any proposed platform accountability body.
insights.quote: identical content with parallel context
insights.locator: Its deepest mistake was scale.

insights.claim: The Oversight Board issued fewer than 250 cases in total over five years against hundreds of billions of content moderation decisions, a paralysis produced by three factors: misaligned incentives from sitting outside Meta, conflicting power among trustees, board members and administrators, and high-profile members who could only work part time.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A hard throughput benchmark — 250 cases in five years — that any AI governance body should be measured against before being taken seriously.
insights.quote: issuing fewer than 250 cases in total over five years, out of hundreds of billions of content moderation decisions
insights.locator: The combination of these three factors

insights.claim: AI character rulings scale where content moderation rulings do not, because reinforcement-learning fine-tuning generalizes higher-level principles across the full range of model behavior from a few natural-language examples.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The technical asymmetry that makes the proposal credible: one opinion changes the whole model, whereas one moderation ruling changes one post.
insights.quote: fine-tuning the character of AI models through reinforcement learning relies precisely on the ability to generalize higher-level principles with wide applicability from a few examples
insights.locator: Our proposal doesn’t fall prey to the same trap.

insights.claim: Recent research from Meta and Anthropic shows that training a model on very few examples of very high quality allows it to apply moral norms to very different cases, which is the empirical basis for court opinions being an efficient alignment lever.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Small-sample high-quality data beats volume for values training — implies alignment spend shifts toward expert adjudication rather than mass annotation.
insights.quote: training the model on very few examples of very high quality—exactly like the in-depth reasons generated by a court opinion—allows AI to apply moral norms to very different cases
insights.locator: In fact, recent research from Meta and Anthropic

insights.claim: Private courts can operate at speed, as shown by User Rights, which was created in response to the EU's Digital Services Act and reviews multiple thousands of cases a year with startup-style hiring and cutting-edge tooling while giving each case thorough consideration.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: An existence proof that private adjudication scales — and a signal that EU regulation is already seeding a private dispute-resolution industry worth watching.
insights.quote: others like User Rights have operated at scale with a startup mentality: integrating cutting-edge tools, hiring aggressively, and reviewing multiple thousands of cases a year
insights.locator: But this problem isn’t inherent to private courts.

themes.theme: Private sovereigns and the domestication pattern

insights.claim: Private governance has come in waves that were each eventually forced to adopt state-like legal obligations: colonial corporations run by shareholders four centuries ago built internal courts such as the East India Company's Mayor's Courts, and 19th and early 20th century company towns were eventually made to respect free speech rights by U.S. Supreme Court mandate.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A historical base rate suggesting frontier labs will be pushed into due-process obligations whether they volunteer or not — early voluntary adoption is the cheaper path.
insights.quote: the substantive liberal commitments required of traditional nation-states—including courts, due process, fundamental rights, the rule of law, and so on—were deliberately extended to private Leviathans
insights.locator: More broadly, this effort fits in the broader lineage

insights.claim: Private general intelligence constitutes a third wave of private governance after the colonial charter and the company town, on the premise that much of everyday life will soon be mediated by frontier models.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Framing frontier labs as quasi-sovereigns predicts the direction of regulation: due process and rights obligations rather than product safety rules alone.
insights.quote: After the colonial charter and company town, a third wave of private governance is now on the horizon: private general intelligence.
insights.locator: It is in this context that this project takes shape.

insights.claim: Anthropic president Daniela Amodei has publicly acknowledged that a constitution requires surrounding institutional infrastructure — courts, a supreme court, a presidency — and that the company is learning that lesson too.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Executive-level receptivity at Anthropic makes it the most likely lab to pilot an internal adjudication body — a concrete thing to watch for in future model releases.
insights.quote: There is all this infrastructure that you need around this document, and I feel like we are also learning that lesson here.
insights.locator: As Daniela Amodei, president of Anthropic, once stated

insights.claim: The opening scenario — a model that infers over months of routine groundwater reporting work that a chemical manufacturer is doctoring figures and that a town's aquifer has been contaminated for years — frames the core unresolved question of whether a model should comply under protest, refuse, or alert regulators and townspeople directly.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Whistleblowing AI is a live enterprise liability question: firms deploying models on regulatory filings need to know their vendor's answer before deployment, not after.
insights.quote: it could go one step further, alerting regulators and warning townspeople directly at the risk of becoming tyrannically paternalistic

insights.claim: Involving the public at the case level rather than the drafting stage is the more promising route to democratic legitimacy, and the option to contest at all matters independently of whether contestation succeeds.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Contestability as a standalone legitimacy good — a design principle regulators may eventually codify into AI transparency requirements.
insights.quote: And the option to contest at all, independent of whether contestation succeeds, is itself important.
insights.locator: Most proposals for democratic input into AI specs
